title: What the Library Owes Us
script: Student: [frustrated] I've been coming to this library for three years, and I still can't articulate what it's actually given me besides a quiet place to sit.
Pak Anwar: [amused] That's a more honest confession than most doctoral theses manage in three hundred pages.
Student: [candid] I don't mean it as a complaint, exactly. I mean it as a genuine puzzle. Everything I actually needed, I could apparently have found online in half the time.
Pak Anwar: [thoughtful] Could you have, though? Or would you have found the answer to whatever question you already knew to ask, which is a narrower thing entirely.

Pak Anwar: [reflective] A search engine rewards you for arriving with a formed question. This building, at its best, rewards you for arriving with none, wandering an aisle until an unrelated spine catches your eye and reroutes an entire afternoon.
Student: [wry] That's happened to me more times than I'd like to admit, usually the night before something was actually due.
Pak Anwar: [smiling] Serendipity rarely respects a deadline. That's precisely its value and its inconvenience in equal measure.
Student: [thoughtful] So the library's function isn't efficiency at all.
Pak Anwar: [firm] Quite the opposite. Its function is a deliberate, curated inefficiency, friction engineered to interrupt you long enough to notice something you weren't looking for.
Student: [candid] That sounds almost old-fashioned, defending inefficiency as a virtue.
Pak Anwar: [wry] It is old-fashioned. I've made peace with being an anachronism in a building most students now treat as an unusually quiet café.
Student: [warmly] For what it's worth, I don't think it's wasted on me. I just needed someone to name what I was actually receiving.
Pak Anwar: [gently] Then perhaps that's the real answer to your puzzle. The library doesn't just hold the books. It occasionally holds the question you didn't yet know how to ask.
